# Introduction

This analysis took data from the Cresko lab at the Univeristy of Oregon which analysed the expression of 600 genes in 80 fish that came from two different backgrounds (labeled as A or B). Each background was treated to two different microbiotic enviornments (conventional or mono). This analysis will load in the data set, map out all of the genes along mean expression and standard deviation between individual fish. From this analysis, genes with unusually high variability were singled out to look at their specific expression across the two backgrounds and microbiomes. This code is written out as a qmd which means that it is reproducable, with full access to the codes and dataset on github.

# Set up
The following code will load the data from the Cresko Lab's public git repository.
```{bash}
#| label: Loading in dataset
mkdir -p  ~/hw2_alex/{data,results,scripts}
curl -L -o ~/hw2_alex/data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv https://wcresko.github.io/BioE_Comp_Tools_Fa2026/Data_Folder/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv
```

The dataset should now be loaded in, with each line representing an individual fish, and each column giving the count expression of 600 genes. In order to use this dataset for analysis, it needs to be both transformed into long data format so that each line is the expression of a single gene for each fish, and then log-transforming the gene counts.

```{r}
#| label: loading packages
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
```
```{r}
#| label: transforming data into long format
out_dir <- "./data"
raw_data <- read_tsv("./data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv")
range <- 5:ncol(raw_data)
long_fish <- pivot_longer(raw_data, 
    cols = range, 
    names_to = "Gene",
    values_to = "Expression") #defines the value or measurement
write.csv(long_fish, file.path(out_dir, "long_fish.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: log transformation
log_long_fish <- long_fish |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), log))
write.csv(log_long_fish, file.path(out_dir, "log_gene_expression.csv"),  row.names = FALSE)
```

# Data analysis

## Plotting genes based on mean and standard deviation

Highly variable genes (HVG) can be identified by plotting the mean and variant expression of each gene. This was calculated in @tbl-summary and plotted out in @fig-mean-sd-plot. HVG are going to be of interest because these genes are likely being **differentially expressed between fish**. These genes will be later analysed to see whether genotype or microbiota condition are able to explain this heightened variability. 

Variability will be calculated using the standard deviation function built into the `dplyr` package under `summarise`. 
$$ \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary

summary_table <- long_fish |>
    group_by(Gene) |>
     summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(Expression),
            sd = sd(Expression),
            median = median(Expression),)
    write.csv(summary_table, file.path(out_dir, "gene_expression_summary.csv"),  row.names = FALSE)
```
```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary-log
log_fish <- summary_table |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), log))
write.csv(log_fish, file.path(out_dir, "log_gene_expression_summary.csv"),  row.names = FALSE)
```
```{r}
#| label: fig-mean-sd-plot
#| fig-cap: "**Varience of gene expression increases as mean gene expression increases. Each point represents one of the 600 genes that were counted for all 80 fish."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot_dir <- "./results"

HVG_plot <- ggplot(log_fish, aes(x = mean, y = sd)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#4A5759") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#EDAF88") +
  labs(title = "Stickleback Highly Variable Genes", subtitle = "expression counts are log-transformed", x = "Mean expression", y = "expression varience")
```
```{r}
#| label: saving fig-mean-sd-plot
ggsave(file.path(plot_dir, "Stickle_HVG.png"), plot = HVG_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

## Finding genes with high variability

@fig-mean-sd-plot shows that there is a strong positive correlation between mean expression and the expected variance of each gene. There are however, a few genes that sit higher above that line of best fit, which can be singled out and labeled to determine the most variable genes. 

In order to do this, the expected variance was calculated for each gene's mean value, meaning that the code will yeild the y value that will fall exactly on the line of best fit for $y = $mx + $b $. The actual standard deviation was then subtracted from the expected distribution and transformed into units of standard deviations. The `high` value can be changed, but a threshold of 1.5 yeilds the top 12 HVG which can be seen in @tbl-dist_z.
```{r}
#| label: tbl-dist_z
resid_df <- summary_table |>
  mutate(fit_sd  = predict(lm(sd ~ mean)),
         dist    = sd - fit_sd,
         dist_z  = dist / stats::sd(dist),
         high    = dist_z > 1.5) |>
  ungroup() 
write.csv(resid_df, file.path(out_dir, "resid_df.csv"),  row.names = FALSE)
```

## Plotting out the top HVG

These genes can now be labeled into @fig-mean-sd-plot to visualize where these HVG are, and to verify that the equations worked. This is printed out in @fig-HVG. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-HVG
#| fig-cap: "**Figure one with HVG points now highlighted and labeled based on filtering for more than 1.5 sd units above the expected sd."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
library(ggrepel)

HVG_plot <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = mean, y = sd)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = dist_z > 1.5), size = 2,) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#EDAF88") +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(resid_df, dist_z > 1.5),
                  aes(label = Gene)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#B0C4B1", "TRUE" = "#4A5759"),
                     guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Stickleback Highly Variable Genes", subtitle = "expression counts are log-transformed", x = "Mean expression", y = "expression variance")
```
```{r}
#| label: saving fig-HVG
ggsave(file.path(plot_dir, "Labeled_Stickle_HVG.png"), plot = HVG_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

# Isolation of top four variable genes

Using the data from @tbl-dist_z the top four genes were isolated; Gene280, Gene361, Gene448, and Gene526! 

## Getting mean and standard deviation summary of top HVG
```{bash}
#| label: data set isolating only genes of interest
cd ./hw2_alex/data
grep -E "Gene280|Gene361|Gene448|Gene526|median" gene_expression_summary.csv > four_fish.csv
```

## Comparing expression of HVG across microbiota and genotype

@fig-four-genes plots out the four genes of interest based on their log expression.

```{r}
#| label: fig-four-genes
#| fig-cap: "**Plots the distribution of expression of the four most variable genes based on their genotype and microb background. Each point represents one fish with violin plot representing density of points at a certain expression level."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
four_fish_violin <- log_long_fish |>
  filter(Gene %in% c("Gene280", "Gene361", "Gene448", "Gene526")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Genotype, Expression, fill = Microbiota)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, color = NA, position = position_dodge(0.8)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = Microbiota), alpha = 0.6, size = 1.2,
             position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.08, dodge.width = 0.8)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.7) + scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ Gene, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Host genotype", y = "Read count of each gene",
       title = "Stickleback gut RNA-seq of four most variable genes",
       subtitle = "Each point is one fish; violins show the full distribution") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```
```{r}
#| label: saving fig-four-genes
 ggsave(file.path(plot_dir, "My_gene_violin.png"), plot = four_fish_violin, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

# Discussion

For each of the four genes, there seemed to be differences in expression based on microbiome group, with the magnitude of differences changing based on genotype. A standard t test would need to be performed to conclude whether any of these changes in expression are actually signifigant. Interesting results include that **Gene 361** showed increased expression in the mono microbiota group, especially in genotype B. **Gene 526** also yeiled unexpected results with drastically different expression levels in the conventional A group compared to the other three fish groups. Further analysis on these particular genes and their background may reveal how fish genotype backgrounds can contribute to how they respond to different microbiota enviornments. 

# Methods

Dataset was loaded in from the Cresko Lab public git repository and processed using `dplyr` in r to get mean and standard deviations. All plots were then generated using `ggplot2`. This specific analysis was written by Alex Kaplan at the University of Oregon (https://github.com/arkfishing7 "Github")
